cues: A dual-arm robot swings to return a fast serve, planned entirely by model predictive control.
Inside, iLQR solves a rolling optimization: a terminal hitting cost plus running costs.
We modify exactly two terms, each independently switchable.
First, the terminal cost.
Instead of one predicted contact point,
it targets a plus-or-minus fifty-millisecond window of candidates, aggregated by a softmin.
Second, a tube around the predicted trajectory: free inside a twelve-centimeter half-width,
a hinge penalty outside, and along-track slack is free.
Here is the same twelve-meter-per-second serve, same seed: point-target misses; the full method returns it.
Across ninety-eight seeds, the candidate window alone lifts the active-hit rate from
fifty-three point one to eighty-five point seven percent,
a paired gain of plus thirty-two point seven points;
plus seventeen point four at nine meters per second.
Under a shared prediction bias, a twenty-cell perturbation grid at nine meters per second,
the gap narrows: eighty-two point eight, versus seventy-three point nine percent.
But tighten the end-effector speed cap to one meter per second, seven-meter serves,
three hundred ninety-four seeds, and the window turns harmful:
minus eleven point nine points for the window alone,
minus twelve point seven for the full stack.
The tube alone still gains plus five point eight.
Under this budget, widening the target does not help.
Main results freeze simulated time for the first plan: nine hundred twenty-eight milliseconds.
Steady-state replanning runs at a four-millisecond median, within the one-hundred-fifty-millisecond budget.
Without freezing, a nine-hundred-ninety-nine-millisecond plan leaves no time to swing.
Which relaxation helps depends on the available execution speed: cost design should follow the speed budget.
